# Controlled Markov stochastic approximation {#sec-controlled-markov-sa}

## Controlled observations and the slow recursion

Let $\ThetaSet\subseteq\R^d$ carry its Borel sigma-algebra, and let
$(\StateSpace,\mathcal X)$ be a standard Borel state space, for example a
Polish space with its Borel sigma-algebra. For each $\theta\in\ThetaSet$,
let $\Ptheta$ be a Markov transition kernel on $\StateSpace$, with
$(\theta,x)\mapsto P_\theta(x,A)$ measurable for every $A\in\mathcal X$.
Let $H:\ThetaSet\times\StateSpace\to\R^d$ be measurable and write
$\Htheta(x):=H(\theta,x)$.

On a filtered probability space, take $(\theta_n,X_n)$ to be
$\cF_n$-measurable and impose the controlled Markov condition

$$
X_{n+1}\mid\cF_n\sim\Pstepn,
\qquad n\geq0.
$$ {#eq-controlled-transition}

For a measurable function $f$, the frozen kernel also acts as an operator:

$$
\Ptheta f(x)
:=\int_{\StateSpace}f(y)\,\Pkern{\theta}{x}{\dd y}.
$$ {#eq-frozen-kernel-operator}

Equivalently, @eq-controlled-transition says that

$$
\E\!\left[f(X_{n+1})\mid\cF_n\right]
=\Pthetan f(X_n)
$$ {#eq-controlled-operator}

for every bounded measurable $f$. The same identity holds for nonnegative
$f$, allowing extended values, and for integrable $f(X_{n+1})$.
For vector-valued functions we apply the operator componentwise.

Given deterministic positive gains $(\gamma_n)_{n\geq1}$, the basic
stochastic approximation recursion is

$$
\theta_{n+1}
=\theta_n+\gamma_{n+1}H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1}).
$$ {#eq-controlled-sa-recursion}

The gain $\gamma_{n+1}$ sets the slow parameter scale, while $P_{\theta_n}$
generates the next observation. Thus the parameter both determines the
observation law and is updated from that observation: the feedback is
$\theta_n\longmapsto P_{\theta_n}\longmapsto X_{n+1}
\longmapsto\theta_{n+1}$. The recursion is required to remain in
$\ThetaSet$; ensuring this and proving stability, or introducing a
stabilisation mechanism, are separate tasks.

## Frozen invariant marginals and the ordinary mean field

Fixing $\theta$ gives a homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel
$\Ptheta$. By contrast, @eq-controlled-transition uses the changing,
history-dependent parameter $\theta_n$; the observations alone need not
form a Markov chain on $\StateSpace$.

::: {#asm-frozen-invariant-marginal}
## Frozen invariant marginal and integrability

For each $\theta\in\ThetaSet$, choose an invariant probability $\pitheta$
for $\Ptheta$, and suppose

$$
\pitheta\Ptheta=\pitheta,
\qquad
\int_{\StateSpace}\norm{\Htheta(x)}\,\pitheta(\dd x)<\infty.
$$
:::

Here invariance means $\pitheta(\Ptheta f)=\pitheta(f)$ for every bounded
measurable $f$. This assumption supplies a reference marginal, not a
mixing rate or uniqueness. If several invariant probabilities exist,
the field below depends on the specified choice. Measurability and
regularity of that choice as $\theta$ varies are additional questions.

Under @asm-frozen-invariant-marginal, define the ordinary frozen mean field
by

$$
\htheta
:=\meanfieldtheta
=\int_{\StateSpace}\Htheta(x)\,\pitheta(\dd x).
$$ {#eq-ordinary-mean-field}

The centred observable is $\bar H_\theta(x):=\Htheta(x)-\htheta$.
Consequently $\pitheta(\bar H_\theta)=0$, but
$\bar H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1})$ need not have conditional mean zero given
$\cF_n$: the conditional law in @eq-controlled-transition is
$\Pstepn$, not $\pi_{\theta_n}$.

::: {#rem-common-invariant-target .remark}
## A common target in adaptive MCMC

In the adaptive-MCMC special case one has $\pitheta\equiv\pi$, so each
frozen kernel preserves the same target $\pi$. This alone does not make
the adaptive observations stationary at finite times. In particular,
when the kernel choice depends on the observed history, common invariance
does not by itself propagate the marginal $\pi$ through that choice,
even if $X_0$ has law $\pi$.
:::

Classical controlled Markov SA seeks conditions under which the weighted
accumulation of $\bar H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1})$ becomes negligible over bounded
intervals of SA time. Together with stability and suitable regularity,
this connects the slow recursion to the ODE

$$
\dot\theta=\htheta.
$$ {#eq-base-ode}

No such approximation or convergence theorem is asserted here.

## The frozen stationary path law

For fixed $\theta$, the stationary finite-dimensional distributions
specified by $\pitheta$ and $\Ptheta$ extend on this standard Borel space
to a two-sided stationary Markov chain $(X_k^\theta)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$.
Denote its law on $(\StateSpace^{\mathbb Z},\mathcal X^{\otimes\mathbb Z})$
by $\statlawtheta$. Its one-time marginal is $\pitheta$ and its forward
transition kernel, conditional on the entire past, is $\Ptheta$.

These two probability laws have different domains: $\pitheta$ describes
one state, whereas $\statlawtheta$ describes an entire trajectory and
therefore its temporal dependence. The path law is not in general a
product law. For an ordinary one-step observable only its marginal
matters:

$$
\Eunder{\statlawtheta}{\Htheta(X_0^\theta)}
=\meanfieldtheta
=\htheta.
$$ {#eq-stationary-one-step-field}

History-dependent variables will instead be defined as functions of the
stationary path. Expectations under $\statlawtheta$ always refer to this
frozen construction, not to the law of the adaptive observations.

## Poisson equation notation

For a measurable function $g_\theta:\StateSpace\to\R^d$, the frozen
Poisson equation is

$$
g_\theta-\Ptheta g_\theta
=\Htheta-\htheta
=\bar H_\theta.
$$ {#eq-base-poisson}

The operator is that of @eq-frozen-kernel-operator. To indicate its role,
suppose a jointly measurable solution family is available, with the
identities valid on the visited states and the required integrability.
Then @eq-controlled-operator gives a martingale difference
$\Delta_{n+1}:=g_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1})
-(\Pthetan g_{\theta_n})(X_n)$.
Substitution into @eq-base-poisson yields

$$
\bar H_{\theta_n}(X_{n+1})
=\Delta_{n+1}
+(\Pthetan g_{\theta_n})(X_n)
-(\Pthetan g_{\theta_n})(X_{n+1}).
$$

After multiplication by gains and summation, the last two terms give
boundary, gain-variation, and parameter-change remainders by summation
by parts. Existence of $g_\theta$, its growth bounds, and its regularity
in $\theta$ are later hypotheses or proof obligations. Invariance alone
does not provide these properties or control the remainders.

## SA time and the ODE language

For the ODE description take $\gamma_n\to0$ and
$\sum_{n\geq1}\gamma_n=\infty$, in addition to positivity. Set

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_0&=0,\qquad t_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\gamma_k,\\
\bar\theta(t)
&=\theta_n+\frac{t-t_n}{\gamma_{n+1}}
  (\theta_{n+1}-\theta_n),
\qquad t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sa-interpolation}

For a general $\ThetaSet$, the straight segments in
@eq-sa-interpolation need not remain in $\ThetaSet$. Applying the
following definition requires a domain containing the interpolated path
on which the ODE has a continuous semiflow.

::: {#def-apt}
## Asymptotic pseudo-trajectory

Suppose @eq-base-ode generates a continuous semiflow
$\Phi:[0,\infty)\times D\to D$ on a domain $D\subseteq\ThetaSet$.
A continuous path $\bar\theta:[0,\infty)\to D$ is an *asymptotic
pseudo-trajectory* (APT) of $\Phi$ if, for every $T>0$,

$$
\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{0\leq s\leq T}
\norm{\bar\theta(t+s)-\Phi_s(\bar\theta(t))}=0.
$$
:::

Thus each late finite-horizon segment follows the ODE started from its
own initial point. Well-posedness of the ODE, stability of the
interpolation, and the noise estimates needed for this property remain
to be verified; the definition itself supplies none of them.

Ordinary controlled Markov SA therefore has the one-step frozen mean
field $\htheta=\meanfieldtheta$ of @eq-ordinary-mean-field. The next
section asks what happens when the update is first passed through a
stable linear memory.
